title: How Déjà Vu Works
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explain déjà vu: its definition and the origin of the term (Émile Boirac, 1876), Freud's repressed-memory explanation, the modern split into associative and biological déjà vu (temporal lobe, epilepsy, schizophrenia), Robert Efron's double-sensory-input delay theory, Alan Brown and Elizabeth Marsh's subliminal-exposure "cell phone" theory, the Darren Brown subliminal advertising stunt, Hermann Snow's hologram memory theory, Arthur Funkhouser's precognitive dream study, and jamais vu. The episode also includes sponsor reads for Audible, a blog plug, and listener mail corrections (Korean unlucky numbers, Tom Selleck in Coma).

segments.title: Opening banter and listener suggestion
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter, including a cotton swab aside, and introduce deja vu as a topic suggested by listener Peter Harrison.

segments.title: Definition of deja vu and personal experiences
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh define deja vu, its French origin and naming by Émile Boirac in 1876, and share personal experiences; they note that roughly 60 to 70 percent of people report having it.

segments.title: Freud and the paranormal history of deja vu
segments.summary: Freud's theory that deja vu results from repressed memories dominated the twentieth century. Deja vu was later linked to the paranormal, which scientists dismissed.

segments.title: Functional MRI and renewed research
segments.summary: Functional MRI revived scientific interest in deja vu, and the research is recent, with theories still competing.

segments.title: Associative versus biological deja vu
segments.summary: Deja vu is split into associative deja vu, which is brief and common among healthy people, and biological deja vu, which is more vivid and tied to brain impairment such as epilepsy or schizophrenia.

segments.title: Temporal lobe and Robert Efron's timing theory
segments.summary: The medial temporal lobe processes conscious memory. Robert Efron proposed that sensory input reaches it by two routes, and a longer-than-normal delay between them can confuse the brain's sense of context, producing deja vu.

segments.title: Subliminal exposure and the cell phone theory
segments.summary: Alan Brown and Elizabeth Marsh showed subliminal photos of locations, which later felt familiar. Brown's cell phone theory says unattended sensory input is processed unconsciously and later triggers familiarity. Stress and rest were both linked to deja vu in different studies. Darren Brown's subliminal advertising stunt is also described.

segments.title: Hologram memory theory
segments.summary: Hermann Snow's theory compares memory to a hologram, where a small fragment can be reconstructed incorrectly, producing a sense of having been somewhere before.

segments.title: Precognitive dreams and jamais vu
segments.summary: Arthur Funkhouser's precognitive dream study is described, along with the idea that forgotten dreams could explain deja vu. The hosts then cover jamais vu, the loss of familiarity with a familiar thing, using the eggs Benedict example.

segments.title: Audible sponsor read
segments.summary: Audible is promoted as a sponsor offering a free audiobook download at audibletpodcast dot com slash stuff.

segments.title: Blog plug, listener mail, and sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck promotes the stuff you should know blog. Listener corrections cover Korean unlucky numbers and Tom Selleck in Coma. The hosts close and point listeners to the article by Leanne Oppenheimer.
